title: Builder Defect Outbreak Radar From Permit Clusters
one_liner: Epidemiology for houses: read repair-permit clusters by builder, subdivision and vintage to tell HOA boards they have a defect outbreak and how many months remain on the legal clock.
customer: HOA management companies and reserve-study firms (about $99-250 per community per year, or a $750 one-time scan). Independent home inspectors and buyer's agents in new-build subdivisions ($19-39 per address). Later, home-warranty companies and homeowners insurers as data licensees.
problem: Production-home defects (roofs, windows, stucco or siding, plumbing, foundations) show up as patterns, but each owner sees only their own house. Boards learn late. Statutes of repose and limitation for construction-defect claims typically run roughly 6-10 years depending on state and quietly expire. Buyers pay for the defect discount without knowing why, and the MLS says nothing.
solution: Ingest city and county permit data. Use an LLM to classify messy permit text (re-roof, window replacement, siding or stucco remediation, re-pipe, foundation or pier repair, water-intrusion repair). Tie parcels to subdivision, builder and year built from plat and assessor data. Compare repair-permit rates to age-matched control cohorts in the same metro. Flag statistically significant outliers. Deliver a 'Community Defect Scan': map, cohort comparison, estimated time left under the applicable state statute (information, not legal advice), and next steps (independent engineer, reserve study update, attorney consult). Also offer a per-address flag API for inspectors.
why_now: The 2020-2022 building boom, built under labor and material shortages with substitutions, is now 4-6 years old, when defects surface and the earliest repose clocks start closing. Permit portals and open data are far more digitized than five years ago. LLMs make classification of messy permit text nearly free. Insurers and lenders are increasingly sensitive to new-build condition.
revenue_model: Community scans at $750 one-time. Management-company portfolio subscriptions at $99-250 per community per year. Per-address inspector add-on at $19-39. Data licensing to warranty and insurance underwriters. Flat fees only, with no referral fees to law firms, to avoid fee-splitting problems.
non_obvious_insight: Individual defects are invisible, but outbreaks are not. Appraisers watch this pattern for years without a feed: neighbors all re-roofing in year 5, three permits for the same water-intrusion fix on one street. The payer isn't the buyer, it's the board with a ticking legal deadline and a manager who wants to look proactive. The trick that makes a 'builder X is an outlier' claim defensible is controlling for age, since old-house repairs are normal and only age-matched cohort comparison isolates the builder.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with clean open permit data and heavy 2019-22 production building (for example Denver suburbs, Phoenix East Valley or Austin/Round Rock). Build the pipeline over about 200 subdivisions. Produce 10 free scans for community managers. Have counsel review the wording (state permit counts and method only, no accusations). Pitch 5 management companies and 3 reserve-study firms, and sell the first 10 scans at $750.

title: Corner-Shop Human Fallback for Age Assurance
one_liner: A network of licensed retailers that check ID in person and mint reusable, privacy-preserving age credentials, sold to age-assurance vendors and platforms as the human appeal layer.
customer: Age-assurance vendors and platforms (social, gaming, adult, gambling, app stores) that face false rejections. Retailers such as independent pharmacies, post offices, newsagents, liquor stores and credit unions earn per credential.
problem: Facial age estimation has error bands near the threshold, so borderline users (16-18, and adults who look young) are blocked. Adults with expired or mismatched ID are locked out. The appeals queue is expensive support, and the legal exposure is real: Australia's under-16 social media law, in force since December 2025, carries fines up to A$49.5 million, and the UK's Online Safety Act requires highly effective age assurance.
solution: Partnered counters run a clerk app. The customer shows government ID, the app reads the chip by NFC without retaining an image, and it issues a reusable over-13, 16, 18 or 21 credential to the person's phone wallet, or a code for those without a smartphone. Platforms and vendors route estimation failures and borderline users to the nearest counter or a video-call agent through one API. Audit logs, retailer training and mystery-shop QA back the process.
why_now: Australia's guidance treats reusable age credentials, vouching and trusted third-party attestation as acceptable methods. California's app-store age assurance law takes effect on January 1, 2027, and UK enforcement has expanded through 2026. Every platform is discovering that automated estimation needs a human fallback.
revenue_model: The vendor or platform pays $0.75-2.50 per rescued user, and the retailer keeps about 40%. Add cents per reuse verification, and enterprise contracts for fallback capacity.
non_obvious_insight: Regulators demand highly effective age assurance, but nobody has built the cheap human appeal layer. Licensed retailers are already trusted age checkers for alcohol, tobacco and medicines. The network of humans is the moat, not the cryptography, and it earns as long as automated estimation is imperfect.
first_30_days: In one Australian metro, sign 40 independent pharmacies and newsagents. Build the clerk app on an open-source NFC reader for passports and licenses. Pitch two age-assurance vendors on a white-label fallback and charge per rescued user for a 60-day pilot. Track false-reject recovery rate as the headline metric.

title: Government Property Control Kit for New Defense Makers
one_liner: A fixed-price property-system-in-a-box (tags, procedures, mock audit, reconciliation) that keeps first-time defense manufacturers from failing their government property audit and having payments withheld.
customer: New-entrant defense manufacturers (drone, munitions second-source and component startups) and small machine shops that receive government-furnished property, plus primes that flow the property clauses down and want their subs certified.
problem: Contractors holding government-furnished property must run a property management system with receiving reports, physical inventory, loss and damage reporting, and reconciliation to the contract's property list. If the government disapproves the system, contracting officers can direct payment withholds. Small shops run this on spreadsheets and no one is the accountable hand-receipt holder. Property administrators cannot coach, and consultants bill $200-400 an hour.
solution: A packaged offering. A one-day on-site 'mock property system analysis' run by former property administrators. Asset tagging and mobile scanning. Templated procedures, forms and a monthly reconciliation to the contract property list. Audit-ready binder and annual physical inventory support. Ongoing loss/damage/destruction reporting and excess-property disposition paperwork. Position it to program managers, not compliance officers, as schedule protection.
why_now: The Revolutionary FAR Overhaul rewrote Part 45 (Government Property), with model deviation text implemented from November 2025, so many contractors are rereading their obligations. Defense spending and drone and munitions ramp-ups are pulling venture-backed hardware companies and first-time subs into contracts with government-furnished property. CMMC phase-ins compete for the same small compliance budgets, so property control gets ignored until an audit finds it.
revenue_model: Mock audit at $6-15k, then $500-2,000 a month for software plus fractional property-officer support, plus per-asset tagging fees. Prime-sponsored programs where a prime pays to certify its sub base.
non_obvious_insight: The property system is about 90% behavior and 10% software: who signs for what, and whether there is an unbroken trail from receipt to disposition. Auditors find the same handful of deficiencies again and again (no receiving report, no physical inventory, no reconciliation, no loss report), so a checklist-driven fixed-price service works better than custom consulting. The strongest sponsor is the prime, because a sub's disapproved system threatens the prime's own schedule and cash.
first_30_days: Pull first-time awardees from SBIR/STTR winners and public contract awards that carry government-furnished property. Offer 10 of them a $2,500 one-day GFP health check. Publish a one-page 'seven findings auditors keep writing' as lead magnet. Partner with a regional APEX Accelerator for referrals and a CMMC registered provider organization for cross-sell. Turn the first 3 engagements into a templated binder and a simple scanning workflow before building any software.

title: Konbini Pulse: Owner-Run Launch Verdict Panel
one_liner: A paid panel of convenience-store owners who report real shelf sell-through of new items in the first 48 hours after each Tuesday launch, sold to food makers who otherwise see only HQ's verdict.
customer: Small and mid-size food and beverage makers, including OEM and private-label suppliers and exclusive-item partners of the big three chains, at ¥150k-500k per brand per month. Later customers are ad agencies, trend and product-development teams, and investors who follow listed food companies.
problem: Every chain launches dozens to hundreds of new items on Tuesdays. An item's fate is effectively decided in 3-10 days, and HQ decides listing and delisting on its own data. The maker, who invested in a line, packaging and ingredients, sees only what HQ tells them. Owners see the real signal: stock-out times, leftover at closing, repeat buyers versus first-day curiosity, counter comments, and differences between office districts and residential areas. That information is never shared with the supplier. Makers cannot tell whether a delisting was fair, so they cannot negotiate.
solution: A 30-second phone routine for each owner: photograph the shelf at fixed times on days 1, 2 and 3, log leftover count at the disposal scan, and tap one of a few reasons customers gave. The panel of 40-150 stores across chains and neighborhoods is aggregated into a '48-hour verdict' delivered to the maker by Thursday: sell-through curve, sell-out time, leftover, repeat rate, and buyer profile by district type. It uses shelf observations and the owner's own counts, not HQ system exports, to reduce contractual risk. Owners are paid monthly, so the panel is a new income line that does not depend on royalty.
why_now: Ingredient and rice inflation has squeezed maker margins, so a failed launch is more expensive than before. SKU churn is accelerating. Japan's revised subcontract law, in force since January 2026, tightens buyers' duty to negotiate prices with commissioned manufacturers, so evidence has value in negotiations. Alternative-data buyers and product teams have no view into konbini shelves, because chain POS data is proprietary.
revenue_model: Subscription per brand, ¥150k-500k a month, plus ¥50k per launch report for smaller makers. Custom studies and delisting-defense reports cost ¥300k-1M. Owners receive ¥8-15k a month in cash plus a revenue share. Aggregate trend data is licensed to agencies and investors.
non_obvious_insight: Suppliers are structurally blind because the only party that counts their sales is the party that decides their fate. The owners standing at the shelf are the only independent observers, and they are invisible to the market because no one pays them. Once owners are paid to observe, the supplier's negotiating position changes. The moat is a trusted network of owners, not software. Data that comes from a shelf photo and a leftover count is less exposed to franchise confidentiality clauses than POS exports.
first_30_days: Recruit 12 stores across the three chains in Osaka through owner chat groups and the franchisee union, paying ¥10k a month each. Build a phone app that takes shelf photos on a schedule and captures counts in a few taps. Choose the next Tuesday launch wave and produce one '48-hour verdict' for five Osaka-area makers with konbini exclusives, offered at ¥50k per launch. Get legal review of the franchise contract clauses on data before scaling. Convert three makers to monthly subscriptions by day 90.

title: Loss-Draft as a Service for Servicers
one_liner: After a hail or wildfire claim, insurer money is trapped in slow servicer loss-draft processes. Digitize milestone releases so contractors get paid in days, not months.
customer: Mortgage servicers' loss-draft departments, and roofing and repair contractors who work insurance claims.
problem: Insurance claim checks are co-payable to the mortgage lender. Servicers hold the funds and release them in draws after inspections, taking weeks to months. Contractors demand money upfront, homeowners run out of patience, and disputes spread (State Farm hail-claim lawsuits are widening from Oklahoma).
solution: Digital loss-draft. The homeowner uploads the claim payment, funds sit in a servicer-controlled escrow, and milestone releases are verified via geo-tagged photo and video review. Contractors are paid instantly via RTP or FedNow, and the servicer gets a compliance dashboard on cycle times.
why_now: Claim disputes are surging and State Farm is adding 3,000 claims staff (Insurance Journal, 2026-09-25). Instant rails are mature, and servicers face regulatory scrutiny on loss-mitigation timelines (verify the specific rules).
revenue_model: $150-$400 per claim from the servicer, or 0.5-1.0% of proceeds, plus a 1% instant-pay fee to contractors.
non_obvious_insight: Servicers hold large claim balances but run loss-draft as a paper-heavy cost center. Contractors accept lower prices for fast, certain payment, which also lowers repair cost and dispute rates.
first_30_days: Approach five mid-size servicers' loss-draft heads with a free diagnostic on average days to disbursement. Sign a pilot for one catastrophe event. Recruit roofing contractor associations in hail-prone states to onboard.

title: Costly-Commitment Kits for Fitness Congregations
one_liner: A retention product for boutique gyms and run clubs that borrows religion's real community mechanism, costly commitment, to turn members into a congregation.
customer: Owners of boutique fitness studios, CrossFit boxes, climbing gyms and multi-site run clubs, with franchisors as the scale channel.
problem: Gen Z made up 47% of new gym joins in 2025 yet posts the highest churn (around 54% in one industry dataset), and nearly half of them say community is why they stay. Studios respond with discounts, apps and easier joining, which attracts free-riders and does not build attachment.
solution: A kit of printed rites, a coach's liturgy guide and light software: an initiation for a founding cohort, attendance vows made to a partner, earned 'colors' for milestones, a dawn 'vigil' class, rites for return-from-injury and for a member's death, and a warm leaving ritual. We A/B the kit across studios against controls on 90-day retention.
why_now: ABC Fitness's 2025 year-end report shows Gen Z dominating new joins and community as a top reason to stay. Run clubs and studios are already positioned as a substitute for church, and retention is the KPI that owners pay to move.
revenue_model: $199-499 per month per studio for the kit and software, a performance option of about 10% of measured retention gains, and licensing to franchisors across their locations.
non_obvious_insight: The whole industry builds community by removing friction, while religious sociology (Iannaccone's 'Why Strict Churches Are Strong') finds that commitment, sacrifice and visible costs create strong communities and free-rider filters. Add cost that feels like meaning (time, visibility, obligation) instead of a fee and members become attached, so the friction studios fear is the mechanism.
first_30_days: Recruit five studios from one local franchise. Run a founding-cohort covenant for new joiners and compare 90-day retention against control cohorts. Publish the result and pitch it to franchise developers.

title: Agent Purchase Warranty: The Liability Layer
one_liner: Everyone is building payment rails for shopping agents. Nobody owns what happens when an agent buys the wrong thing, so sell the warranty and dispute layer.
customer: Startups building AI procurement and shopping agents for small businesses (office, restaurant and parts supplies), and the merchants those agents buy from. The first buyer is an agent vendor that wants merchants to accept its agent.
problem: Visa, Mastercard, Coinbase, Ripple and Stripe are all in agentic rails, and Visa and Mastercard joined Rain's alliance on 2026-08-18. Chargeback rules assume a human clicked buy. ISO's generative-AI exclusion is spreading across CGL policies, so when an agent orders 40 cases instead of 4, the merchant says it was authorized, the bank agrees, and the insurer excludes it.
solution: A mandate-versus-receipt adjudication API. The user's signed intent mandate (budget, item class, merchant allowlist) is logged. On a dispute, the API compares mandate, cart, receipt and delivery and pays valid claims automatically. The first version is a reserve-backed service warranty capped at $500-$2,000 per order, later fronted by an MGA and carrier. Merchants who accept mandate-logged agent orders get a 'warranted agent' signal that cuts false declines.
why_now: Agentic payments alliances formed in Aug 2026, DoorDash is live on Stripe/Tempo, and AI exclusions are appearing on thousands of CGL policies (Insurance Business, 2026-09-16). Transaction volume is arriving just as coverage disappears.
revenue_model: Per-order warranty fee of about 0.4-1.0% of order value from the agent vendor or user. Merchant-side acceptance fee. Later, MGA commission once a carrier fronts the risk.
non_obvious_insight: Rails are commodity and crowded, but liability allocation is what decides trust, just as Stripe won by absorbing fraud and disputes rather than moving bytes. Insurers exclude 'AI' generically because they have no data. A signed mandate log is exactly the data that lets a small underwriter price a slice they can't.
first_30_days: Pick one SMB-procurement agent vendor. Offer a free mandate-log SDK plus a capped $50k reserve-backed warranty on its first 500 orders, and record dispute types and rates. Use that loss data to sign three similar vendors at about 0.75% per order.

title: Dixie Flatline for Retiring Plant Operators
one_liner: Neuromancer's Dixie Flatline (a dead expert preserved as a consultable construct) built for retiring water and plant operators, with consent, clip-grounded answers and royalties paid to the expert.
customer: Municipal water and wastewater utilities, rural electric co-ops and small chemical or food plants, reached through state rural water associations and funded by state workforce and infrastructure grants.
problem: A large share of plant operators is nearing retirement, and the knowledge that matters is tacit ('when pump 3 hums like that in the cold, do this'). SOP binders miss it, experts sandbag because they fear being replaced, and a hallucinating chatbot is unacceptable when chlorine dosing is involved.
solution: A three-week Walkdown Capture: the expert tours the plant with a chest camera and mic, thinking aloud. Their answers are aligned with SCADA and alarm history so past incidents can be replayed ('what did you do in the January freeze?'). Structured critical-decision interviews feed a queryable construct that answers only with citations to the expert's own clips, deployed on a tablet or radio for night operators. The retiree signs a consent and royalty agreement, is paid per consult, can revoke, and remains reachable as a paid human escalation.
why_now: Utilities are in the middle of a retirement wave, and cheap wearable cameras, speech-to-text and retrieval systems make capture-and-query affordable for a small team. Regulators and grant programs increasingly fund workforce succession.
revenue_model: $20-45k per capture project, $1-3k per month hosting per plant, and a royalty share passed through to the expert.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not modeling but eliciting and compensating. Experts hide knowledge when the goal is replacement, and paying them a revocable royalty flips the incentive. Grounding every answer in the expert's own clips solves the hallucination problem and makes the tool defensible with regulators and insurers.
first_30_days: Ask three state rural water associations for introductions. Run one pilot with a retiring operator for $5k or free, and produce a short demo of a construct answering a night-shift question with clip evidence. Aim for three paid projects by month six.

title: Employer-Backed Workforce Pell Program Packager
one_liner: Package 8-15 week, employer-guaranteed training programs that clear state approval and the 70% completion and 70% placement tests, paid per verified hire by the employers who need workers, with Pell covering tuition.
customer: Employers with chronic shortages (HVAC contractors, utilities and lineworker programs, hospitals for phlebotomy, CNA and sterile processing, machine shops, CDL trucking) paying per hire. Community and technical colleges are the Title IV-eligible partners.
problem: Workforce Pell (from 1 July 2026) opens Pell Grants to 150-599 clock-hour programs. A governor and state workforce board must approve each program as aligned to high-skill, high-wage, in-demand jobs, and programs must show at least 70% completion and 70% job placement plus a tuition-versus-earnings test. Colleges' continuing-ed divisions lack employer partnerships, placement tracking and approval paperwork skills. ED approved its first programs in mid-Sept 2026 (Nebraska, Texas, North Carolina) and 36 jurisdictions have an operating process.
solution: Act as a program packager and placement-assurance layer, not a tuition-share OPM, given the Title IV incentive-compensation rules. Steps: co-design the syllabus from employer job tasks; assemble the state approval dossier with employer letters and labor-market data; give the college cohort software covering employer offer commitments contingent on completion, completion nudges, and 180-day placement tracking via payroll and wage-record attestations; and bill employers per successful hire rather than per enrollment.
why_now: The program is only weeks old, states are just standing up approval processes, and the outcome thresholds will remove weak programs. Colleges need employer-tethered programs that can actually hit the 70/70 tests.
revenue_model: $2,000-$6,000 per hire from employers (well below typical 15-25% agency fees), $1-3k/month per college for cohort and placement software, and fixed fees for approval dossiers.
non_obvious_insight: The outcome test flips the customer. The college's real risk is the 70% placement rate, and only an employer that pre-commits to hire can guarantee it, so the payer is the employer rather than the student or school. Pell effectively becomes a federal training subsidy for whichever employers organize demand first.
first_30_days: Pick one state with a live approval process and shortages (Texas, North Carolina or Nebraska) and one sector such as HVAC, lineworker or sterile processing. Collect 5 employer hiring commitments and co-apply with 1-2 community colleges for a 10-week program. Run a non-Pell pilot cohort while approval is pending to test placement, and have counsel review the incentive-compensation boundary.

title: Agent-Populated Simulated First Job for Juniors
one_liner: A 12-week simulated first job where new grads work inside a persistent fake company staffed by AI coworkers, clients and managers, producing an auditable work record employers trust.
customer: Employers pay $4-8k per hire or subscribe to pre-screened cohorts. Universities and bootcamps pay per-seat licences ($500-1,500), and state workforce boards fund seats. Start with RevOps, FP&A or customer-success analyst roles.
problem: The bottom rung is gone. Employers don't hire juniors because AI absorbs the tasks they learned on, and internships or apprenticeships need employer bandwidth, the very thing missing. Grads can't get the experience employers demand (Stanford: 19% gap, 42% underemployment).
solution: A persistent multi-agent world with a messy CRM or ledger, a ticket queue, stakeholder agents with hidden goals who change requirements, an AI manager giving 1:1s and an on-call incident. The junior works with their own AI tools and everything is logged. Senior humans grade a few deliverables weekly. The output is a portable 'experience ledger' (hours, artifacts, review outcomes, error-detection rates) employers can inspect.
why_now: Long-horizon agent capability and multi-agent simulation now make believable coworkers affordable (Project Vend-style and TheAgentCompany-style experiments), employers say they can't evaluate candidates in AI-permitted interviews, and the freeze is widening.
revenue_model: Employer per-hire success fees and pre-screen subscriptions, university licences and modest learner fees.
non_obvious_insight: The cold start of apprenticeship marketplaces is employer supply. A simulation removes it: the employer is fake but the evaluation is real. Employers hire on traces of judgment rather than resumes, and the moat is a scenario library built from anonymised real incidents.
first_30_days: Build one role sim (RevOps analyst) with 4 agent personas. Run it with 20 recent grads via a college career centre. Get 5 mid-size SaaS employers to review the graduates' traces and commit to interviews.

title: Deadline-Proof AI Overflow and PII Shield for CPA Firms
one_liner: A browser extension that strips client SSNs, EINs and bank numbers before any AI tool sees them, and routes work to a compliant pay-as-you-go model when the firm's licensed AI hits its usage cap in the middle of a deadline.
customer: Accounting, tax and bookkeeping firms with 3 to 30 people, plus the MSPs that run their IT. All of them have written-security-program duties under the FTC Safeguards Rule.
problem: In 2026 vendors are moving to usage-based AI billing (Microsoft now uses Copilot Credits with administrator spending limits). When a firm's tool hits its cap mid-deadline, staff face three options: work stops, costs climb, or they improvise with personal consumer accounts. Uploading client statements and spreadsheets to unvetted tools breaks the Safeguards Rule's service-provider oversight requirement. Firms have no visibility into what left the building.
solution: A lightweight extension and gateway. First, it detects client PII (SSNs, EINs, account and routing numbers, dates of birth) in prompts and uploads and swaps in reversible tokens, with the mapping kept locally on the user's device. Second, it meters each seat's usage against the firm's licensed tools and, at 80% of a cap, offers an approved overflow route to a zero-retention model API billed at wholesale token cost plus a margin. Third, it writes an audit log that maps directly onto the firm's written information security program: who used what, which data classes were blocked, and which vendors were approved. Pre-purchased burst capacity is sold before each crunch (Oct 15 extension deadline, Mar 15, Apr 15).
why_now: The relevant CPA Practice Advisor article is dated Sept 28, 2026 (today). The Oct 15 extension deadline is 17 days away. Usage-based AI billing became normal this year. Firms are cutting headcount but software costs don't fall with it, so overflow spend competes with shrinking budgets.
revenue_model: $19 per seat per month for the shield and audit log, plus metered overflow at token cost +30%. Burst-capacity packs of $99 to $499 per season. MSPs and state CPA society partnerships get a channel margin of about 20%.
non_obvious_insight: The risk is not the AI model, it is the capacity cliff at the worst possible moment, which pushes careful staff into shadow tools. CPA Practice Advisor states: 'When a firm's AI tool hits its usage cap mid-deadline, staff often turn to free consumer tools', cites the FTC Safeguards Rule requirement for a written information security program and oversight of service providers, and quotes IBM's finding that high shadow-AI usage adds about $670,000 to breach costs, with 63% of breached organizations having no AI governance policy (https://www.cpapracticeadvisor.com/2026/09/28/token-limits-are-creating-a-shadow-ai-problem-for-accounting-firms/190633/). A companion piece shows why buying more seats isn't the answer: software costs stay flat when headcount falls, with contracts fixed until the notice deadline (https://www.cpapracticeadvisor.com/2026/09/03/why-client-software-costs-dont-fall-when-headcount-does-and-what-advisors-should-review/189557/).
first_30_days: Week 1: build the redaction extension for Chrome/Edge with regex plus a small detector, and a simple metering dashboard. Pitch it in accounting communities and state CPA society newsletters as a 'get through Oct 15' tool. Weeks 2 to 3: onboard 10 firms free for the extension season in exchange for testimonials and audit-log feedback. Week 4: convert to $19 per seat and sell burst packs ahead of the next crunch; approach two MSPs that serve CPA firms. Target: 8 paying firms and 1 MSP partner.

title: Contingency Royalty Audits for Game Developers
one_liner: A $99 automated statement check that finds provable underpayments in publisher royalty reports, then hands winnable cases to forensic accountants on contingency.
customer: Developers signed with publishers who are unrecouped or getting opaque quarterly statements. They pay $99-299 for the check and 20-25% of any recovered money. Referral fees also come from games lawyers and auditors.
problem: Audit clauses exist in most publishing deals (one analysis found them in 88% of deals with an advance), but a formal audit costs more than a small studio can recover, so publishers effectively face none. One 30-contract analysis found 42% gave the publisher 100% of revenue until recoupment. Marketing 'recoupables', vague net-revenue definitions, cross-collateralization and FX and VAT handling all hide errors. Devs sit on a spreadsheet they can't verify.
solution: Devs upload the contract and statements. We rebuild the recoup waterfall from the contract's own definitions and compare it with independent signals: review-count unit estimates, price history and regional mix. We flag anomalies such as marketing above a cap, taxes deducted twice, giveaway keys counted as spend, and FX gaps. A clause pack and a negotiation script push new deals toward Steamworks read-only financial permission for the dev. Flagged cases go to a panel of forensic accountants who send a formal audit notice.
why_now: The 2023-25 layoffs pushed thousands of devs into 'marketing-only' publishing deals with recoup terms. LLMs can now parse contracts and statements at near-zero marginal cost. Funding is tight, so every unpaid royalty matters.
revenue_model: Flat pre-audit fee, 20-25% contingency on recoveries (cheaper than the roughly 40% litigation contingency), and referral fees from lawyers. Later: a paid tier for funds and lenders that want portfolio royalty monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: Detection was never the bottleneck. Cost was. A cheap pre-audit that separates provable errors from noise lets an auditor take only winnable cases. Publishers in a small, gossipy industry often settle quickly once a credible notice lands, because they don't want the precedent to spread, and many errors are honest spreadsheet mistakes.
first_30_days: Launch a free recoup-waterfall calculator and a 'publisher-deal red-flag scan' on r/gamedev and dev Discords. Collect about 100 anonymized statements as training and proof data. Sign referral deals with two games-industry lawyers and one forensic accountant. Take the first 5 contingency cases with flagged anomalies over $10k.

title: Stomach-Ready: GLP-1 Protocols for Endoscopy Centers
one_liner: An intake, coaching and point-of-care gastric ultrasound service that stops GLP-1 patients from turning up to endoscopy with a full stomach and getting cancelled on the table.
customer: Independent GI practices and ambulatory surgery centers (ASCs) that run 5-30 endoscopies a day, plus anesthesia groups that staff them. The buyer is the medical director or administrator.
problem: GLP-1 drugs slow gastric emptying. Studies in 2026 show retained gastric contents in roughly one in five endoscopy patients on the drugs, and some procedures are aborted. Guidance has moved from 'stop the drug for a week' to 'continue it, use a 24-hour clear-liquid diet, do selective gastric ultrasound and communicate across teams'. Centers have no operations layer to run this. Front-desk staff cannot tell who is on which drug, at what dose or when the last injection was. Surprises happen day-of, causing cancelled slots, rebooking, extra anesthesia risk and idle rooms.
solution: A text and portal intake flags GLP-1 users (brand, dose, weekly or daily, last injection date, symptoms). It auto-assigns the guideline-based protocol, sends coaching and adjusts dose timing per the clinician's rules. It flags high-risk patients (dose escalation phase, gastroparesis symptoms) for a 90-second gastric POCUS on the day. A travelling RN sonographer or a trained center nurse does the scan with a handheld device, and the result goes straight into the anesthesia record. Phase 2 adds AI-assisted image reading.
why_now: A April 2026 wave of studies (residual gastric content 'far higher than expected') and updated multi-society guidance made continue-and-modify the new standard, which needs new workflows. Oral Wegovy and orforglipron are about to widen the user base. Procedure centers are squeezed on throughput and cannot afford dark rooms.
revenue_model: $15-30 per GLP-1 patient screened and coached, plus $60-100 per gastric ultrasound performed. Alternatively a flat $500-1,500 per site per month. One avoided aborted case is worth roughly $1k+ in recovered slot revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The expensive problem is not the rare aspiration event, it is aborted cases and scheduling chaos. Guidelines supplied a protocol but nobody supplies the operations layer that knows which day of the week each patient injects. The physician societies are a free distribution channel once a protocol is written up.
first_30_days: Get 2-3 GI ASCs on a free 60-day pilot and measure their baseline aborted and rebooked rate. Have a GI and an anesthesiologist advisor sign off on a protocol drawn from published guidance. Build the intake on Twilio and a simple form. Buy two handheld ultrasound units (about $3-5k each) and contract an RN sonographer for spot coverage. Then convert the pilot sites to paid.

title: Swimmer-Distress Drones for Endurance Events
one_liner: A race-day service using thermal-camera drones and AI to spot swimmers in trouble before rescue boats do.
customer: Triathlon, open-water swim and Ironman-style race directors, event insurers, and municipalities running beach swims.
problem: Most triathlon deaths occur in the swim, and safety still depends on kayaks and volunteers scanning choppy water. A study at the 2018 IRONMAN Mont-Tremblant found drones identified 1 of 5 distress events before rescue boats saw them, and human spotters tire.
solution: An operator-plus-software service: one or two drones with visible and thermal cameras track the swim course, AI flags prolonged stillness, vertical posture or flailing, and alerts go to the rescue coordinator by radio app, with a post-race report for insurers. Later add wearable tags and AED delivery.
why_now: Thermal drone cameras and edge vision models are cheap, FAA rules for wider drone operations are advancing, and open-water race participation is climbing.
revenue_model: $2.5-8k per event, annual series contracts, and insurer-funded discounts.
non_obvious_insight: The pain sits with event insurers and small race directors, for whom one fatality can end the event, so the pitch is loss reduction with data. AI is valuable mainly because it does not get tired.
first_30_days: Buy two drones (about $8k), recruit a licensed Part 107 pilot and a lifeguard consultant, provide free coverage at two local swims to collect labeled footage, and pitch 10 small triathlon directors a $1.5k pilot.

title: ILIT Rescue After the Estate-Tax Cliff Disappeared
one_liner: A paid, documented review of irrevocable life insurance trusts built to pay estate tax that most families will never owe.
customer: Trustees (individuals and bank or trust companies), estate attorneys, and families holding ILITs with policies of $1M-$25M.
problem: For decades planners sold ILITs to fund federal estate tax. With the reported $15M-per-person exemption from 2026 (verify), many of these families will never owe it. Trusts keep paying premiums on policies that may be unnecessary, underfunded or poorly performing. Trustees fear fiduciary liability for doing nothing, yet nobody is paid to run the review.
solution: A 'trust-policy triage' service. Ingest the trust document and in-force illustration, classify the trust's purpose, and produce a decision memo: keep, reduce, 1035-exchange, sell, decant or terminate. It documents a prudent-process file for the trustee. Then execute through licensed partners (settlement broker, insurance agency, trust counsel).
why_now: The 2025 tax law reportedly raised and indexed the exclusion. About 10M life policies lapse per year (per the brief's cited market data), and the life-settlement market has active buyers (Coventry, Abacus). Wealth flows to heirs are large enough that leaving policy value on the table is now visible.
revenue_model: $2,500-$7,500 review fee per trust plus success fees on settled or exchanged policies where licensing allows.
non_obvious_insight: Fiduciary duty turns optimization into a mandatory review: trustees are exposed if they do nothing, so someone must be paid to produce the file even when the answer is 'keep'.
first_30_days: Recruit 2 estate attorneys and a licensed life-settlement broker. Pitch corporate trustees' special-assets desks. Run 10 reviews at a $1,500 intro price and learn which outcomes come up most.

title: First-72-Hours Concierge for Paid Communities
one_liner: An outcome-priced service that staffs experienced ex-power-mods to personally handle every new member's first three days in creator-run paid communities, cutting the week-one churn that drains recurring revenue.
customer: Owners of paid communities with 500-20,000 paying members on Skool, Circle, Discord, Mighty Networks or Patreon: course creators and trading, fitness and business coaches doing $50k-$1M+ per month.
problem: Skool operator guides say about 60% of churners decide in week one, and average monthly churn sits around 12-18%. Owners cover the front door with random volunteers or VAs posting templated welcomes. New members' first posts go unanswered for a day. Scam DMs from fake admins ('send USDT to verify') hit newcomers hardest. The first unexplained removal or cold reply turns a paying member into a refund request.
solution: Small pods of trained ex-moderators run the first 72 hours: a personal welcome, a reply to every first post within 2 hours across time zones, routing to the right thread, removal of impersonators and scam DMs, and gentle handling of first-time rule breaks so the person stays. AI drafts and triages, but a human always sends. Each community gets a rules-as-code playbook and a weekly cohort-retention report with a holdout group so the effect is measurable. Work stays on Discord, Skool and Circle, so it doesn't collide with Reddit's Rule 5.
why_now: Reddit began enforcing its five-community moderator cap on 31 March 2026. That has pushed many experienced volunteer mods into Advisor/Alumni roles and left them open to paid work on platforms the cap doesn't cover. Creator-run paid communities have grown into real revenue businesses, while AI slop and scam DMs make the new-member experience worse.
revenue_model: A base fee of $1.5k-$4k per month per community plus an outcome kicker of 10-20% of retained MRR uplift versus a holdout. Mods are paid $15-$25 per hour, giving roughly 40-50% gross margin.
non_obvious_insight: In big subreddits a newcomer whose first comment is removed without explanation almost never returns. Retention is decided in the first three days by one human interaction, not by content quality. That makes moderation a retention function, not a cost center, so it should be priced by churn saved, not hours worked. It is also hard to outsource to a generic trust-and-safety BPO, because tone and judgment are the product.
first_30_days: Recruit 10-15 ex-power-mods from mod Discords and r/ModSupport who lost seats under the cap. Write a one-page playbook. Approach 30 owners of Skool communities with 1k+ paying members, using the public discovery listings. Offer a $750, 14-day pilot in which half of new joiners get the concierge and half don't. Report the day-14 retention delta and convert the best results into monthly contracts.

title: Notary Network for Human-Verified Hiring
one_liner: Bonded local human witnesses (mostly mobile notaries and loan-signing agents) sit with a job candidate for a phone-free live work sample and sign an attestation the employer can rely on.
customer: Remote-first companies of 20-2,000 people hiring for roles that touch code, money, patient data or production systems (fintech, health-tech, cybersecurity, engineering, back-office BPO), plus staffing and recruiting agencies placing remote workers. The first buyer is a 30-person startup that cannot fly candidates to HQ.
problem: Video interviews are no longer trustworthy evidence of who is doing the work. Real-time face-swaps, proxy test-takers and AI feeding answers are common: a 2026 Greenhouse survey reportedly found 91% of US hiring managers had encountered or suspected AI-generated answers, and Gartner projects that by 2028 one in four candidate profiles will be synthetic. Google and McKinsey reportedly reintroduced in-person verification steps, but a small remote employer cannot fly every finalist in, and detection software is an arms race the defenders keep losing.
solution: A marketplace of vetted, insured, background-checked local witnesses. The candidate meets one at a library room or coworking space. The witness checks government ID in person, hands the candidate a locked-down laptop or a paper packet, and stays through a 60-90 minute live work sample or technical interview run by the employer over the employer's own video call. No phones are allowed in the room. The witness signs a notarial-style attestation (ID match, unbroken presence, session log, photo) that goes into the employer's applicant file. Sold as a $150-250 per-session add-on to the final-round interview. The same primitive later extends to bootcamp and university oral exams, licensing bodies, and witnessed authorship for authors and artists.
why_now: In 2026, deepfake candidates are ranked among the top fraud threats by Experian, and hiring teams are openly adding in-person checks. Meanwhile mortgage volume is still well below its 2021 peak, so tens of thousands of trained loan-signing agents have idle capacity and already know how to verify identity and witness a signature. Remote notarization and gig onboarding tools make a distributed 1099 witness network cheap to stand up.
revenue_model: Employers pay $150-250 per attested session (witness keeps roughly 55%). Subscription tiers for volume hirers ($500-2,000 per month with session credits). Enterprise and staffing-agency contracts with bulk pricing. Later: per-exam fees from education and credentialing bodies.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not better deepfake detection but a cheap, trusted, physical human at a known place, and the law already has an institution for that: the notary. A loan-signing workforce is already trained, insured and idle. The purchase also gets filed under fraud and insider-risk compliance (nation-state fake-IT-worker schemes, SOC 2 evidence) rather than HR, which means bigger budgets and faster approval.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 signing agents in three metros through notary Facebook groups and NotaryCafe-type forums, with a simple 1099 onboarding. Write the session protocol and attestation PDF in a week; run booking and payment with Airtable and Stripe. Cold-email 100 remote-heavy startups and staffing firms with the offer 'we will send a human to sit with your finalist, first 3 sessions at $99'. Aim for 10 paid sessions by day 30. Publish an anonymized case study of the first mismatch or coached-answer catch.

title: Data-Center Community Benefits That Fund Rural Vets
one_liner: An intermediary that packages animal-care compacts (vet loan repayment, mobile clinics, low-cost care days, shelter energy upgrades) as community-benefit commitments for data-center developers fighting local opposition.
customer: Data-center developers and hyperscaler community-affairs teams siting campuses in rural and exurban counties, plus county officials. Payment is a program management fee on the pledged benefit package.
problem: Seven in ten Americans oppose data centers in their community (Gallup) and New York has imposed a statewide hyperscale moratorium. Delays are extremely costly (a delayed 60 MW commissioning costs about $14M a month). Typical community benefits are abstract (tax revenue, school grants). Meanwhile rural counties face a vet shortage (91,100 US vets, only about 3,100 openings a year) and vet costs are the single most visible affordability pressure for pet and livestock owners.
solution: Design and run a neutral 'Vet Access Compact' per county: loan repayment or salary top-ups for rural vets and techs, a solar-battery mobile clinic, quarterly low-cost vaccine and spay/neuter days, and shelter energy upgrades. Administer it with measurable outcomes (appointments, wait times), match it with philanthropic dollars where possible, and give the developer credible, publishable reporting. Optionally link the developer's backup power to the clinic's resilience.
why_now: Data-center opposition and moratoria surged in 2026, and electricity affordability is a midterm issue. Duffield's $250M commitment and PetSmart Charities' pledge provide matching money. New vet-professional tiers (Colorado's VPA) expand who can be funded.
revenue_model: 10-15% program design and administration fee on $1-5M multi-year packages, grant-matching and outcome-reporting retainers, and implementation fees for mobile clinics.
non_obvious_insight: Animals are one of the few bipartisan, hyper-local issues that reach every county, and a $2M program is a rounding error against a $1B campus. It pairs capital-rich, trust-poor developers with trust-rich, capital-poor local vets who also speak at public hearings.
first_30_days: Pick 3 counties with pending data-center hearings on the public calendar. Call the county veterinary association and extension office to map the gaps. Produce a one-page compact and pitch it to developers' community-affairs leads. Sell a $15-30K design study as the first paid engagement. Avoid contingent fees tied to permit outcomes.

title: Private Road Associations in a Box
one_liner: Turn the neighbors' informal, cash-in-a-coffee-can road fund into a recorded, insurable road association with dues, reserves and competitively bid plowing and grading.
customer: Households on private roads and shared driveways (5-60 homes per road). The urgent buyers are the real estate attorneys, title agents and listing agents whose closings stall without an enforceable road maintenance agreement.
problem: Millions of rural households reach their homes by private roads maintained by handshake. One neighbor plows, some chip in, some free-ride. Washouts and disputes are common. Lenders and title insurers often want a recorded, enforceable maintenance agreement, so sales stall. HOA software assumes an incorporated HOA with a manager, not 12 neighbors and a gravel road.
solution: Fixed-fee formation: map who benefits, draft a state-specific maintenance agreement, record it with the county, and set up a simple legal entity or association where state law allows. Then recurring service: ACH dues collection with reminders and lien-based enforcement where allowed, a reserve fund, standing bids from vetted plow, gravel and grading contractors, a photo log of road condition, and storm-damage documentation packages for county or FEMA requests.
why_now: Post-2020 in-migration put many remote workers on rural private roads. Extreme-weather washouts, such as Hurricane Helene's damage to private roads and bridges in western North Carolina in 2024, showed how many neighborhoods have no entity that can pool money or apply for repair aid. Lenders and insurers keep tightening property-access checks. No vertical software serves informal neighbor groups.
revenue_model: $1,500-3,000 formation fee, paid by the neighborhood or by the seller at closing. $12-25 per household per month for dues administration. A disclosed 5-8% procurement fee on managed contractor bids.
non_obvious_insight: The customer with urgency isn't the neighborhood but the closing. A failed sale costs a seller and an agent five figures, so attorneys and agents will send you deals for a flat fee. Recurring revenue then comes from dues float and admin. At 200 associations you are the largest single buyer of plowing and gravel in a region, which gives you procurement leverage no individual road has.
first_30_days: Pick a state dense with private roads (Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire, or the North Carolina mountains). Get an attorney to draft a reusable agreement template. Partner with 3-5 real estate attorneys and title agents who see failed closings. Sell a $1,500 'closing rescue' formation package. Run 2 pilot associations with free dues collection for 6 months to prove the workflow.

title: Remote-Driven Tractors for the Door-to-Door Leg
one_liner: Teleoperated tractors, driven from desks by remote drivers, that shuttle trailers between autonomous-truck terminals and customers' docks within about 30 miles.
customer: Autonomous-truck operators that need a handoff solution, carriers with hub networks, shippers with private yards, and ports and rail ramps.
problem: Hub-to-hub autonomy leaves door-to-door legs with 'hundreds of dollars' of human transfer cost per handoff, yet most freight is door-to-door. Short-haul and drayage driver turnover is high.
solution: Start on private yards, where no on-road rules apply, with retrofit teleop kits, multi-carrier connectivity and automatic safe-stop on link loss. A remote driver handles moves back to back with no deadhead, and automation covers straight segments. Extend later to short, permitted public-road hops at low speed. Price per move below a local yard driver plus deadhead.
why_now: Aurora (about 200 driverless trucks, 30,000 planned), Einride and Gatik are scaling the hub model, and the handoff economics are unresolved. Remote driving has been operating commercially in Europe and Las Vegas, and multi-carrier bonding makes latency manageable. Public-road legality for teleoperated heavy trucks in the US is unclear and needs checking.
revenue_model: $/move pricing, a monthly retainer per terminal, and equipment lease on the retrofit kits.
non_obvious_insight: The industry frames the last leg as an automation problem, but it is a utilization problem. One remote driver can serve several times more moves than a local driver who deadheads between yards, so teleop can beat both a human and a full autonomy stack on price for the next several years.
first_30_days: Sign a private yard (a rail ramp or DC with 20+ yard moves a day), retrofit one tractor with a rented teleop kit, and run a week of shadow operations. Price the pilot at about 20% below the current yard-jockey cost.

title: Peer-Made Aide Training in Creole, Spanish, Tagalog
one_liner: A library of short scenario videos made by experienced home-care aides in their own languages, RN-reviewed and sold to agencies as required in-service training that keeps new aides from quitting.
customer: Home-care agencies, home health agencies and nursing homes in immigrant-heavy states (NY, FL, MA, NJ, CA). The buyer is the training or HR lead, paying per aide.
problem: Agency turnover runs 77-80% and roughly 4 in 5 new caregivers quit within 100 days. 30% of direct care workers are immigrants (60% in New York), and about 350,000 Haitians lost TPS on Aug 4. Federal rules require annual in-service hours for home health aides and nursing-home nurse aides (12 hours a year, and states add more), and most content is English-language corporate e-learning or AI-dubbed avatars that workers ignore and that can be clinically wrong.
solution: Recruit working aides who already post in Haitian Creole, Spanish, Tagalog or Arabic on Facebook, TikTok and WhatsApp. They shoot 3 to 6 minute scenarios (transfers, dementia redirection, refusing a bath, safe lifting). An RN reviews each script, and the clip carries a 'peer-made, RN-verified' provenance stamp. The platform adds quizzes, attendance logs for surveyors, and a first-week mentor-video track aimed at the 100-day cliff. Creators get 35-40% of revenue plus a bonus for completion.
why_now: Visa pauses and TPS terminations are reshuffling the workforce by language group right now. The federal nursing-home staffing mandate was repealed (Feb 2026), which leaves retention as the agencies' only lever. AI slop training content is flooding the market, and creators are hunting for income beyond ad revenue.
revenue_model: $9-14 per aide per month billed to the agency (a 75-aide agency pays about $700-1,000), sold as an annual contract. About 35-40% goes to creators. A later add-on covers state-approved CE credits and dementia-training modules.
non_obvious_insight: Aides do not quit because training is bad. They quit because nobody who looks or sounds like them says the job gets easier. A peer in your language who has survived the first 100 days is a retention device that also happens to satisfy a compliance line item, and an AI avatar cannot supply that credibility.
first_30_days: Find 5 aide-creators through Creole, Spanish and Tagalog Facebook groups and workforce training programs. Partner with a per-diem RN reviewer. Shoot 20 scenarios in 3 weeks and pitch 5 agencies (start with Miami, Boston and NYC) on a 90-day pilot at a free-first-month price tied to a measured 100-day retention improvement.

title: Reserve-Crew Backup Photographers for Wedding Day Emergencies
one_liner: A paid-standby bench of pre-vetted, style-matched backup photographers who can be dispatched within 2-3 hours, sold to solo photographers as a subscription and to wedding insurers as claims fulfillment.
customer: Solo and small-studio wedding photographers ($199-399/yr for a 'Continuity Guarantee' they can promise couples), plus wedding-insurance carriers and MGAs that cover vendor failure but cannot produce a person.
problem: Every solo photographer's nightmare is a sudden illness, crash or family emergency six hours before a wedding. The standard backup plan in contracts is 'a photographer friend', which fails in practice. On peak Saturdays (dates like 10/10/26) every competent local shooter is already booked, so the Facebook SOS post at 6am gets 40 sympathetic comments and zero style-matched, available humans. Whoever does show up has never seen the timeline, venue notes, family-formals list or the photographer's look. Wedding insurance reimburses money after the fact but cannot supply a competent human in three hours. It is a capacity-reservation problem, not an insurance problem.
solution: Members upload style samples plus a 'Continuity Pack' for each booked wedding (timeline, family list, venue and light notes, gallery drop link), all in one place. We maintain a regional bench of vetted shooters tagged by style (documentary, bright and airy, moody, film-look). Bench shooters are paid a small standby retainer (about $40) to hold peak dates, plus an activation fee ($500-900) paid by the member or the insurer. On activation, the pack is pushed to the understudy, a coordinator handles couple communication, and images are delivered under the member's brand. Members display a 'Continuity Guaranteed' badge, which becomes a booking-conversion asset.
why_now: Vendor-failure cover is now a standard add-on in wedding insurance, and 2026 contracts increasingly require a comparable replacement or a full refund, so the gap between reimbursing money and supplying a photographer is now visible and contractual. Weekend supply is squeezed onto peak dates, and a growing pool of freelance portrait, real-estate and second-shooter talent with open weekends can be organized cheaply through Stripe Connect and shared workspaces. Insurers are also under pressure to reduce claim severity in small commercial lines.
revenue_model: $99-399/yr member subscription (tiered by number of weddings), per-activation fee split with the bench shooter (we keep about 20%), and an insurer contract of a flat per-policy fee or per-claim fulfillment fee. Standby retainers are funded from the subscription pool, like airline reserve crews.
non_obvious_insight: Backup fails precisely on the dates it is needed, because scarcity is correlated. The free 'photographer friend' network evaporates on peak Saturdays. The only fix is paying for reserved capacity in advance, and once you do, you own the only reliable answer to the industry's most feared event.
first_30_days: Pick one metro. Sign 25 solo photographers as founding members at $99/yr and recruit 8 bench shooters (portrait, real-estate and second-shooter talent with open Saturdays). Build the Continuity Pack in Notion/Airtable plus a shared Google Drive. Run a fire drill: on a chosen Saturday, ping every member's pack and time how fast each is delivered to a bench shooter. Pitch two wedding-insurance MGAs on a 90-day claims-fulfillment pilot, and get a lawyer to check contractor and liability terms before the first live activation.

title: Population-Diverse iPSC Villages for Drug Safety
one_liner: Pool 50-100 genetically diverse donor iPSC lines in one dish and read out each donor's drug response by genotype, giving pharma a 'clinical trial in a dish' for roughly the cost of one experiment.
customer: Pharma safety-pharmacology and toxicology groups, oligonucleotide and gene-editing developers worried about idiosyncratic toxicity, and NAM-adopting CROs.
problem: The NAM debate centers on organ complexity, but single-donor organoids cannot show the population variability behind idiosyncratic liver injury or QT prolongation. FDA now wants 'adequately validated' methods, and conventional multi-donor testing costs n times as much.
solution: A curated, consented and commercially licensable diverse iPSC panel differentiated to cardiomyocytes or neurons (where villages are best proven), dosed with compound series and demultiplexed by genotype through scRNA-seq. Deliver donor-level dose-response distributions, genotype-linked sensitivity and concordance versus clinical outcomes.
why_now: Village-in-a-dish methods have matured, with CIRM-funded pooled iPSC-cardiomyocyte 'clinical trial in a dish' work and a 2026 methods perspective in Frontiers in Bioengineering. Greenstone Biosciences is an early commercial competitor in cardiac models. The FDA rule gives sponsors a reason to buy, and scRNA-seq costs keep falling.
revenue_model: $60-150k per compound panel, $300k/year subscriptions, and licensing the panel to CROs.
non_obvious_insight: Pooling collapses the cost of diversity: n=100 costs roughly what n=5 does. The moat is the consented, well-characterized line panel and a genotype-linked outcomes database, not the assay, which anyone can copy.
first_30_days: License 30-50 lines from public repositories, checking commercial-use consent. Build a cardiomyocyte village. Test 20 reference cardiotoxic and safe drugs and publish the concordance. Pitch 10 safety-pharmacology leads on $30k pilots.

title: Quibi for Home-Care Aides: Serialized Compliance Training
one_liner: Quibi's 90-second premium episodes failed as a consumer subscription; as a serialized vertical drama that home-care aides watch to fulfill their mandatory annual training hours, the same format has a captive, budgeted buyer.
customer: Owners and training directors of home-health and home-care agencies with 20-500 aides. Medicare-certified home health agencies must give each aide annual in-service training (12 hours under federal rules), and many states add annual hours for personal-care aides.
problem: Caregiver turnover benchmarks around 75% in 2025. Required training is slide decks and quizzes that workers click through on phones, yet client falls, infections, abuse-reporting failures and survey citations trace back to it. Agencies pay for training that neither sticks nor improves retention.
solution: A private serialized story of two aides and a difficult client. Each 90-second vertical episode ends on a decision (dementia sundowning, family conflict, suspected neglect); the answer unlocks the next episode. Delivered by SMS or WhatsApp link with no app, in English, Spanish, Tagalog and Haitian Creole. An RN advisor approves content, quiz logs map to training-hour documentation, and supervisors get a completion dashboard. AI-assisted production plus human voice actors keeps a season at low tens of thousands of dollars.
why_now: Microdrama apps are booming: industry trackers put short-drama in-app revenue near $3B in 2025 and forecasts of roughly $8B in 2026, so the habit and format exist. Reported AI-assisted production budgets of $15-80k per series are far below traditional costs. Home-care demand is surging while the workforce shrinks.
revenue_model: $6-10 per aide per month with a $300/mo agency minimum, annual contracts; bespoke episodes on an agency's own policies at $3-5k each; same engine later sold to nursing homes, restaurants and hotels.
non_obvious_insight: Quibi's format was fine and its buyer was wrong. Consumers would not pay $8/mo for premium clips, but mandatory compliance budgets are captive and the outcomes (completion, quiz retention, incident reports, quits) are measurable. Frontline workers already binge microdramas on the same phones, so the drama does the engagement work and the compliance layer does the billing.
first_30_days: Write 6 episodes on three topics (dementia behaviors, fall prevention, abuse reporting) with an RN advisor and produce them for under $5k. Pitch 30 agencies through state home-care association lists and LinkedIn. Run free 30-day pilots at 3 agencies, comparing completion and quiz scores against their current slides, then convert to $500/mo contracts.

title: Funding Waterfall at the Vet Estimate
one_liner: Front-desk software that routes each vet estimate to the cheapest available funding: insurance advance, charity grant, clinic plan, or credit.
customer: Independent and affordable-care vet clinics as the subscriber. Charitable funds and lenders are paying counterparties.
problem: 85% of vet professionals say clients decline care at estimates of $1,000 or less, and 13% of euthanasias are attributed to inability to pay. Funding sources exist but are fragmented: reimbursement-model insurers pay weeks later, dozens of small charity funds are unknown at the front desk, and mainstream medical credit charges clinics steep fees. New philanthropy has no distribution pipe, so grants like Duffield's are hard to place and audit.
solution: An 'estimate inbox' where the front desk emails or prints the estimate, with no PIMS integration. Within minutes it returns a ranked stack: (1) a 0% claim advance for insured pets secured by the expected reimbursement; (2) pre-screened charity or grant matches; (3) a clinic-carried 0% plan backed by a shared default-guarantee pool; (4) conventional credit. One application, one payout to the clinic in 24-48 hours, with compliance reporting for funders.
why_now: The Duffield Foundation committed $250M over 5 years on Sept 17, 2026 (first grants: 250 x $10K plus $10M multi-year), building on PetSmart Charities' $100M pledge. Neither has pipes for high-volume, low-friction placement. Insurance premiums are up 19.7% against animals up 9%, and clinics are being coached on money conversations. Instant payment rails let clinics be paid the same day.
revenue_model: Clinics pay 1-2% of routed funding or $199 a month. Funders pay about 5% of grant flow as an admin fee, which is cheaper than their own staff. Lenders pay origination fees.
non_obvious_insight: The decline decision is made in a 90-second front-desk moment, and every funding source is built for a different moment. Whoever owns the estimate document owns the routing, and philanthropic money is desperate for a distribution pipe with audit trails.
first_30_days: Sign 15 independent clinics in one metro and run the waterfall as a concierge service with spreadsheets and email. Approach one small pet charity and apply as an infrastructure partner to the Duffield programme. Find one claim-advance lender willing to take insurer-receivable risk on a pilot basis.
